title: Singapore breathes

scenes.text: This is Singapore at night. Colour = people at home. 6.04 million, mostly in the heartlands.
And this is the same city on a weekday morning. Watch the centre inflate — and the new towns drain.
Raffles Place holds ~600 residents at night — and almost 88,000 people by day. Two cities, one map.
Sengkang and Punggol move the other way: tens of thousands leave every morning. Every commute you see on the MRT is this map rebalancing itself.

punchline: Singapore is a living system. The atlas measures its heartbeat.

title: Where the next supermarket goes

scenes.text: Ask a simple question: if you opened ONE new supermarket, where would it win the most customers?
The model weighs every resident, every competitor, and every walking distance — 2.5 million hex-to-hex relationships.
It keeps pointing here: Yunnan, in Jurong West. ~60,000 people, and the nearest supermarket is a long way from most of them.
Here is the part that matters: a separate government-data study found the same gap. The model never saw that study — it found the desert from structure alone.

marks.text: the model's pick = the known desert

punchline: The model never saw the FairPrice study — and found the same desert.

title: Not recombination — new knowledge about the city

scenes.text: This atlas doesn't just collect data — it invents measurements. Here are three maps of Singapore that did not exist before, anywhere.
Map one: people who could reach a new shop on foot — but have NO supermarket near their own home. The surprise winner isn't the heartlands. It's the East Coast.

marks.text: Bayshore — 2,300 in reach, none served at home

scenes.text: Map two: where jobs and workers cannot reach each other. Colour = jobs reachable per reachable worker within 45 minutes of transit. The western industrial fringe burns bright — thousands of jobs, almost nobody who can get to them.

marks.text: Tuas View Extension — 85,000 jobs per reachable worker
Benoi & Gul — the transit gap, quantified

scenes.text: Map three: where businesses go to die. From 2.07 million company records: the share of recently registered businesses already closed. And it doesn't just show WHERE — click any red hex and the site card names the likely driver: thin footfall, rent pressure, crowded trade, or a fragile F&B-heavy mix.

marks.text: Tampines East — 52% of 624 recent businesses closed

scenes.text: Each of these was tested against all ~800 measurements that existed before it. Near-zero overlap — they carry information about Singapore that nothing else does. That is the test of invention.

punchline: Three maps of Singapore that exist nowhere else.
